column1: # Player-facing settings: the iOS launcher (dm/ios/Sources/Launcher.swift) and the Mac app's settings window (dm/mac/Launcher.swift) show them before the game starts; Mac front ends read the same list.

# dm/games/settings.py writes one game's list into its app (dm/launcher.json; build_ipa.sh, and dm/mac/pack_app.py through the NSP script): the rows whose condition holds for that game, with its defaults. Each sets an environment variable the host reads when the game starts; one an env file sets
# (Documents/env.txt, the bundle's dm/env.txt) is shown but kept. Diagnostic switches stay environment-only, so they are not listed here. The player's page is docs/settings.md.
#   variable  the environment variable the setting sets

#   kind      choice: values value=label,..., an option only some games have with ?<shown>&<shown> after its label (languages: the game's own, from its control data; every language when it has none, with a note); range: values low:high:step, shown as a percentage;
#             toggle: values - (on sets 1, off 0) or <on>/<off>, the two values the variable takes (on/off)
#   default   a value (a toggle's: 1 on, 0 off); DM_GAME_<NAME>: the host's own default from the game profile (game_profile.h, game.py); build:<VAR>: the IPA build's setting (build_ipa.sh)
#             <ios>|<mac> selects the platform's default before resolving a profile macro or build variable

#   shown     always; DM_GAME_<NAME>!=<value> or ==<value>; fixups:<KEY>: main's rewriter table has that key (a stub in the game's build, patch_nso.py); languages>1 (more than one to pick, so also when the control data lists none); gfxapi:<API>: the packer's GFXAPI;
#             platform:<ios | mac>: the app's platform (SETTINGS_PLATFORM, ios when unset), for a switch only that platform's front end reads
#   section   Game, Controls or Performance: a heading on the single settings screen. Rows appear in table order within each section
#             Reset to tested defaults clears all launcher choices; values fixed by an env file stay
#   label, note  the setting's name and the line under it (may be empty): its cost (latency, memory, heat), then the setting recommended, as "Recommended: ..."
#   meta      optional, key=value pairs separated by ; (settings.py META lists the keys; docs/frontends.md, The settings list, describes them):
#             level=basic  a setting a front end shows first;  needs=<VAR>=<value>  a sub-setting, drawn only while the row that sets <VAR> has that value

column8: Recommended: 30 fps with Frame generation on. 60 fps heats an iPhone within a few minutes, and iOS then slows it down.

Shows 60 frames a second while the game draws 30: MetalFX makes a frame between each two. Less work and heat than 60 fps, with more input delay than real 60; fast motion can smear. Recommended: on, with Deadline boost, Real-time presenting and Encode thread on.

Lighter makes the in-between frames at 0.75 of the picture's size, and MetalFX scales the picture back up: about half of frame generation's GPU time, for a slightly softer picture, the HUD too. Recommended: Full; Lighter with Wide view on (it makes about a fifth more pixels to fill in), or if frames drop in busy areas.
Adjusts resolution between 70% and 100% under load. Turn off to keep full resolution for the selected console mode. Recommended: off when you set a Render scale.
Recommended: 0.60 on an iPhone. Lower it if frames drop in busy areas: it is the setting that frees the most GPU time.
For iPhones with less memory (8 GB, such as the iPhone 15 Pro): the A builds' memory savers. Off, none of them runs. Recommended: off, unless the game closes on an 8 GB iPhone.
Recommended: Handheld on an iPhone. Docked renders at the TV resolution: heavier, warmer, and little sharper on a phone screen.
Normal renders 1280×720 handheld (1951×1098 docked), steady at 30 fps. Potato is the game's lighter mode: 960×540 shown at 720p, for 60 fps on a warm phone. Recommended: Normal.
Uses more GPU time and can increase heat. Recommended: Standard.
Recommended: MetalFX. It takes about 1 ms where the game's own upscaler takes several.

Fill crops the game's 16:9 picture to cover the screen. Health bars, subtitles or maps near the edges can be cut off. A full-screen picture without cropping needs a patch for each game. Recommended: Fit.
Recommended: off; turn it on to check the frame rate.
The colours of the on-screen controls.

Fills the whole iPhone screen with a wider view and no black bars. Renders about a fifth more pixels and uses more memory: a little slower and warmer. Takes effect the next time the game starts. Recommended: off with Frame generation, on for 30 fps without it.
Renders about a quarter more pixels: a little slower and warmer.

Tells iOS each frame's deadline, so it keeps the game on the fast cores at a higher clock. Uses more power and heat. Recommended: on. Off, a warm phone moves the game to the slow cores and frames drop.
On tells iOS how much of each frame the presenting thread needs, which keeps it fast. Off may use less power, with a risk of more stutter. Recommended: on.
Up to one frame more display latency. Recommended: on. Frame generation turns it on anyway.
Keeps a pipeline archive; uses more memory. Recommended: on: fewer stutters the first time an area is drawn.
The first start waits a few minutes for it, once. Recommended: on.
Prepares each frame's GPU work on a thread of its own. Recommended: on. Off, the game's own thread does it every frame and frames come late, with stutter.

Skips objects the game's visibility checks found hidden a frame earlier, instead of drawing them while this frame's answer is still on its way. Saves GPU time; an object coming into view can appear a frame late. Recommended: off; try it if frames drop in busy areas.
Recommended: off at a fixed 30 fps.
Apple's performance overlay. Costs a little GPU time. Recommended: off; on only to measure.
